newsitem.title: GERMANY: German chemical industry to discuss sick pay.
newsitem.headline: German chemical industry to discuss sick pay.

text.p: German chemical industry employers and the IG Chemie union plan to discuss the issue of sick payments on Friday, two days after a similar summit meeting for the metal industry collapsed.
The two sides, which normally enjoy a relatively harmonious relationship and pride themselves on being able to hammer out their annual wage agreements quickly, will meet in Wiesbaden on Friday.

Earlier this month workers at BASF AG, one of Germany's largest chemical groups and the only large group so far to say it will implement a new law allowing sick pay cuts, walked off the job in protest.
Sources close to the talks said the two sides would try to find innovative ways to solve the sick-payment issue. Other topics are also on the agenda, the sources said.
A statement will be issued after the talks, a spokesman for the employer group BVAC said on Thursday.
Industrial relations in Germany have soured markedly since a law became effective on October 1 allowing employers to cut workers' salaries by 20 percent during illness.

On Thursday hundreds of thousands of metal industry workers laid down tools to protest against the law after summit talks between the IG Metall union and employer association Gesamtmetall collapsed after failing to reach agreement.

This year's chemical industry wage contract specifically allows companies to pare back sick pay, highlighting a difference between the two industries' wage contracts. But an IG Chemie spokesman said no large chemical group has implemented the cuts yet.
BASF AG said it would begin reducing sick pay to 80 percent of the salary on November 1. "We expect the employers will negotiate with us," the IG Chemie spokesman said.
Sources close the employer group said two more summit meetings are planned to discuss the sick pay issue.
One possible avenue for compromise may be to try to reduce the amount of sick time and still pay the full salary, sources said.

Several board members at large chemical companies have recently said that a reduction in Germany's very high rate of sick days taken every year would be far more effective in curbing costs than cutting wages.
The Bonn government passed the law in a bid to save more and meet the entry criteria for Europe's planned currency union.
